title: TypeScript Foundations: Strict Types to Validated Applications
description: A strict beginner TypeScript course covering inference, unions, narrowing, object contracts, typed functions, generics, utility types, runtime validation, testing, and a typed progress-tracker capstone.

Model and narrow primitive, union, object, collection, and generic types safely
Validate unknown runtime data and build a modular typed progress tracker

lessons.title: TypeScript Setup and Type Inference
lessons.summary: Configure a small strict TypeScript project and understand how the compiler infers types from values and reports unsafe operations before JavaScript runs.
objectives: Explain and apply the TypeScript behavior taught in TypeScript Setup and Type Inference
Use strict compiler evidence and runtime tests to verify the contract

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: TypeScript is a static analysis layer over JavaScript. The compiler checks source and emits JavaScript; types do not normally exist at runtime. Start with `tsconfig.json`, enable `strict`, and compile with `tsc --noEmit` during checking. Type inference derives useful types from initial values, so `const count = 3` needs no `: number`. Add annotations at public boundaries or where inference is too broad, not to repeat obvious facts. A compiler error is evidence of a mismatch between operations and declared possibilities; fix the model or narrow the value instead of silencing it with assertions.

lessons.summary: Model values with primitive types and unions, then narrow uncertain inputs through runtime checks before using type-specific operations.

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: TypeScript primitive types include `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `bigint`, `symbol`, `null`, and `undefined`. A union such as `string | number` says either representation is valid. Code must narrow the union before calling operations available to only one member. `typeof`, equality checks, `in`, and discriminant properties provide evidence the compiler can follow. Prefer `unknown` for untrusted input because it requires narrowing; `any` disables checking and lets defects spread. Literal unions such as `'planned' | 'complete'` restrict values more precisely than a general string.

lessons.title: Object Types, Interfaces, and Optional Properties
lessons.summary: Describe object shapes with interfaces and type aliases, distinguish optional properties from undefined values, and preserve excess-property checks.
objectives: Explain and apply the TypeScript behavior taught in Object Types, Interfaces, and Optional Properties
Use strict compiler evidence and runtime tests to verify the contract

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: Object types document required fields and their value types. Interfaces are well suited to extendable object contracts; type aliases can represent objects, unions, primitives, and tuples. `name?: string` means a property may be absent, while `name: string | undefined` requires the property key even when its value is undefined. Mark data immutable with `readonly` when mutation is not part of the contract. Fresh object literals receive excess-property checks that catch misspelled fields. Avoid broad index signatures unless every unknown key genuinely follows the same value rule.

lessons.title: Typed Arrays and Function Contracts
lessons.summary: Use typed arrays, tuples, parameter and return types, optional/default parameters, callbacks, and overload-free union contracts.
objectives: Explain and apply the TypeScript behavior taught in Typed Arrays and Function Contracts

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: An array type such as `number[]` constrains every element, while a tuple records a fixed sequence of positions with distinct types. Function parameter types protect callers and explicit return types protect the implementation's contract. Optional parameters come after required ones; default parameters already behave as optional to callers. Callback types describe both inputs and outputs, enabling methods such as `map` to infer results. Prefer a union parameter when behavior and return type are the same for every member; overloads are useful only when input forms imply meaningfully different output types.

lessons.title: Generics and Standard Utility Types
lessons.summary: Use constrained generics when behavior is independent of a specific type, and derive focused types with Pick, Omit, Partial, and Record.
objectives: Explain and apply the TypeScript behavior taught in Generics and Standard Utility Types
Use strict compiler evidence and runtime tests to verify the contract

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: A generic parameter preserves a relationship between inputs and outputs. `function first<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | undefined` returns the same element type supplied by the caller. Add a constraint such as `T extends { id: string }` only when the implementation uses that capability. Do not introduce a generic used in only one position; a concrete or union type is clearer. Utility types transform existing contracts: `Pick` selects keys, `Omit` removes keys, `Partial` makes properties optional for patch operations, and `Record` maps a known key union to one value type. These are compile-time transformations, not runtime validation.

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: TypeScript cannot guarantee data arriving from JSON, forms, storage, or network responses. Parse external values as `unknown`, inspect their structure at runtime, and only then return a trusted domain type. A type assertion does not validate anything; it merely tells the compiler to trust the author. User-defined type guards return predicates such as `value is ProgressRecord` after checking required evidence. Keep validation at system boundaries and let internal functions operate on validated types. The capstone separates raw input, validation, domain updates, calculations, and presentation so each layer can be tested.
